nameStory: The Hairy Spider Weevil gets its unusual name from its fuzzy, hair-like scales that cover its body and its remarkably long, spindly legs that make it look more like a tiny spider than a typical beetle. Unlike most weevils that are chunky and slow-moving, this species scurries around with surprising speed, adding to its spider-like appearance.
description: The Hairy Spider Weevil is a small, distinctive beetle that's easy to mistake for a spider at first glance. It has the characteristic long snout of all weevils, but what sets it apart are its unusually long, thin legs and body covered in pale, fuzzy scales that give it a frosted appearance. Adults typically measure about 4-6mm long, making them roughly the size of a large grain of rice.

idTips.label: Long spindly legs
idTips.description: Legs are unusually long and thin for a weevil, extending well beyond the body when walking and giving it a distinctly spider-like gait

idTips.label: Fuzzy pale scales
idTips.description: Body appears frosted or dusty due to dense covering of pale, hair-like scales that feel slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Curved snout
idTips.description: Classic weevil rostrum (snout) that's moderately long and curved downward, distinguishing it from true spiders

idTips.label: Quick movement
idTips.description: Moves with surprising speed and agility, often stopping abruptly and remaining motionless when disturbed

idTips.label: Dark underlying color
idTips.description: Beneath the pale scales, the body appears dark brown to black, visible where scales have worn away

habitat: Found primarily in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with rich leaf litter and decaying organic matter. They're most common in oak-hickory forests and forest edges, often hiding under logs, stones, or in loose bark during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active as temperatures warm, often seen crawling on tree trunks and fallen logs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly encountered, actively feeding and mating on various host plants.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek overwintering sites under bark, logs, and leaf litter as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in protected locations and are rarely seen, though warm winter days may bring out a few individuals.

funFact: **Note: Some details about this species may be uncertain due to limited reference material** This weevil can actually drop from trees when disturbed and 'play dead' by tucking in its long legs, making it nearly impossible to distinguish from a small piece of debris until it suddenly springs back to life and scurries away.
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for a small spider due to its long legs and quick movements, but the presence of a weevil's characteristic snout and six legs (instead of eight) quickly reveals its true identity. Remember: 'Snout speaks beetle, eight legs speak spider.'
contextualKnowledge: **Note: Classification details may be uncertain** Despite being called a 'spider' weevil, this beetle is completely unrelated to true spiders and belongs to one of the largest beetle families in the world. The spider comparison is purely based on appearance and behavior.
compareHints: **Note: Comparison details may be uncertain** As the only Exomias species commonly found in New England, it's most easily confused with other small weevils in the Curculionidae family. However, most other weevils have much shorter, stouter legs and lack the distinctive pale, fuzzy scaling that gives this species its frosted appearance.
